name: Battle of Vienna (1683)
info: On 12 September 1683 a relief army of Imperial and Polish forces under John III Sobieski defeated the Ottoman army of Kara Mustafa Pasha at Vienna, after a two-month siege, and the Ottomans were later driven from most of Hungary.

facts.date: 12 September 1683, the last day of a siege that began on 14 July 1683
facts.place: Kahlenberg and the ground north-west of Vienna, then the Habsburg capital, in present-day Austria
facts.sides: The Holy Roman Empire and the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth under King John III Sobieski, with Ernst Rüdiger von Starhemberg commanding the garrison; the relief army is put at 65,000 soldiers with 165–200 guns by one assessment, and at 70,000–80,000 by another. The Ottoman Empire under Grand Vizier Kara Mustafa Pasha, with an army given as 28,400 to 50,000 in the battle
facts.outcome: The relief army defeated the Ottomans and Vienna was saved. The Ottomans fought on until 1699 and lost control of Hungary and Transylvania.

t: The siege lasted two months, from 14 July to 12 September 1683, and the relief army and the garrison together defeated the Ottoman army in a single day.
Strengths are disputed: the Ottoman army in the battle is given as 28,400 to 50,000 men, and the relief army as 65,000 or as 70,000–80,000.
The Ottomans fought on until 1699, when the Treaty of Karlowitz ceded much of Hungary to the Habsburgs.
dyk: Before the siege the Ottoman Empire and the Holy Roman Empire had been at peace for 20 years under the Peace of Vasvár, and the allied cavalry charge on 12 September has been called the largest known cavalry charge in history.
ev: Imre Thököly, reinforced by an Ottoman contingent, is recognised by the Ottomans as King of Upper Hungary
The Ottoman army is mobilised on 21 January and war is declared on 6 August
The Treaty of Warsaw binds the Holy Roman Empire and Poland to mutual support
The main Ottoman army reaches Vienna and Kara Mustafa demands its surrender
The Poles under Sobieski cross the Danube at Tulln to join the imperial troops
The Ottomans occupy the Burg ravelin and the low wall nearby
The relief army attacks and defeats the Ottoman army, ending the siege
The Treaty of Karlowitz cedes much of Hungary to the Habsburgs

sections.background:
Capturing Vienna had long been an Ottoman aim, because the city controlled the Danube and the overland trade routes to Germany and the Eastern Mediterranean. In the years before the siege the Grand Vizier Kara Mustafa Pasha had roads and bridges repaired and had ammunition and cannon sent to depots in the Balkans. For 20 years a peace, the Peace of Vasvár, had held between the two empires.

In Habsburg-held Hungary, unrest had grown into open rebellion against Leopold I's pursuit of Counter-Reformation principles and his wish to suppress Protestantism. In 1681 Protestants and other anti-Habsburg Kuruc forces led by Imre Thököly were reinforced by an Ottoman contingent, and the Ottomans recognised Thököly as King of Upper Hungary. They also promised the Hungarians a Kingdom of Vienna should the city fall. Clashes between Thököly's forces and the Holy Roman Empire grew in 1681 and 1682, and Habsburg incursions into central Hungary gave Kara Mustafa his argument to persuade Sultan Mehmed IV and the Divan to allow the army to move. The sultan authorised him to operate as far as Győr and Komárom. The army was mobilised on 21 January 1682 and war was declared on 6 August 1682.

The 15-month gap between mobilisation and the full invasion gave Vienna time to prepare. Leopold gathered troops and formed an alliance with Poland, Venice and Pope Innocent XI. Under the Treaty of Warsaw of 1683 he promised to support John III Sobieski if the Ottomans attacked Kraków, and the Polish army was to relieve Vienna if it were attacked.
sections.forces:
Figures for the Ottoman side differ. One account puts the army at 28,400 men or approximately 50,000 during the siege, and the whole campaign force at around 90,000, of whom 35,000 were left at Győr and 50,000 went to Vienna. Kahraman Şakul assesses the Ottoman army as approximately 120,000 soldiers and 156 guns, noting that only the household and retinue troops are counted exactly and the numbers of provincial and vassal troops are expected ones. Another estimate has the Austrian ambassador Kunitz giving 180,000 men, a third of them away from the siege. The Ottomans had 130 field guns and 19 medium-calibre cannon. Troops from the vassal states of Transylvania, Wallachia and Moldavia held bridges on retreat routes and did not take part in the battle.

Emperor Leopold left Vienna for Passau with his court, and Charles V, Duke of Lorraine, withdrew his 20,000 towards Linz. The city was held by Ernst Rüdiger von Starhemberg with 15,000 troops and 8,700 volunteers, who had 370 cannon.

Sobieski left Kraków on 15 August. The Lithuanian army under Kazimierz Jan Sapieha campaigned in the Hungarian Highlands instead and reached Vienna only after it had been relieved. Poles and Imperial troops, joined by Saxons, Bavarians, Baden troops and others, took Sobieski as the overall commander. One assessment gives the relief army 65,000 soldiers with 165–200 guns, another 70,000–80,000. Mustafa gave the defence of his rear to the Khan of Crimea, whose cavalry numbered between 30,000 and 40,000.
sections.course:
The siege began on 14 July, when Kara Mustafa sent the traditional demand to surrender, which Starhemberg refused. Food supplies into the city were almost entirely cut. By early September about 5,000 Ottoman sappers had opened gaps about 12 metres wide in the walls, and on 8 September the Ottomans took the Burg ravelin and the low wall nearby. The relief army meanwhile crossed the Danube at Tulln on 6 September and signalled its arrival on the Kahlenberg with bonfires.

At 4:00 am on 12 September the Ottoman army attacked, hoping to disrupt the allied deployment. Charles of Lorraine's imperial army on the left took the fortified villages of Nussdorf and Heiligenstadt after heavy fighting. Kara Mustafa counterattacked with most of his forces but held back some Janissary and Sipahi units for an assault on the city. His sappers had prepared ten mines under the Löbelbastei, but the defenders found and disarmed them. In the early afternoon the Polish infantry advanced on the Ottoman right, and by 4:00 pm the Poles held the village of Gersthof. The imperial forces advanced again from 3:30 pm and took Unterdöbling and Oberdöbling by 5:00 pm, closing in on the Türkenschanze.

At around 6:00 pm Sobieski ordered the cavalry to attack in four contingents, three Polish and one from the Holy Roman Empire. 18,000 horsemen charged down the hills, Sobieski leading 3,000 Polish heavy lancers, the Winged Hussars. The Ottomans, exhausted and demoralised, broke and began to retreat, and the garrison sallied out. Less than three hours after the charge the allied forces had won the battle.
sections.aftermath:
Counts of the Ottoman losses differ. They lost at least 20,000 men during the siege, and in the battle around 15,000 dead according to Podhorodecki, or 8,000–15,000 dead and 5,000–10,000 captured according to Tucker. An Ottoman account captured after the battle lists 48,544 casualties up to 10 September. The relief force lost approximately 3,500 dead and wounded, including 1,300 Poles; Tucker's estimate is 4,500. The Viennese garrison and the civilian population lost about half their number from all causes during the siege.

The Ottomans had also pillaged the countryside. At Perchtoldsdorf, whose people had barricaded themselves in a church fortress and surrendered on a promise of safety, the men were massacred and the women and children enslaved. In total 57,220 people are recorded as taken away as slaves from the Austrian and Hungarian border zone in 1683: 6,000 men, 11,215 married women, 14,922 unmarried women under 26 and 26,093 children.

On 25 December Kara Mustafa Pasha was executed at Belgrade by strangulation, by order of the Janissary Agha. The Ottoman historian Silahdar Findiklili Mehmed Agha called the defeat the most disastrous since the foundation of Ottoman statehood in 1299. Among the allies, tension arose over the loot of the Ottoman camp, since Sobieski claimed first choice, and the Protestant Saxons left at once and refused to continue the pursuit. Sobieski liberated Esztergom after the Battle of Parkany, though dysentery halted his pursuit. Starhemberg ordered the walls repaired at once.
sections.sources:
The Ottoman side is known partly from Ottoman records and partly from Austrian ones, and they differ widely on numbers. An anonymous Ottoman table of siege casualties survives, and Kahraman Şakul argues that only its figures for household and retinue troops are counted, the rest being rounded or expected numbers. Ottoman accounts give the household army as 25,529 Janissaries, 3,045 weaponeers and 4,000 gunners, 32,574 in all, against 60,000 in the table. The Austrian ambassador Kunitz reported what he learned from Ottoman captives. An Ottoman account captured after the battle gives the casualties up to 10 September. The contemporary Ottoman historian Silahdar Findiklili Mehmed Agha wrote of the defeat. Sobieski's own letter to his wife describes the loot.

Several points are disputed. Whether the relief army numbered 65,000 or more is argued: the figure of 68,000 is said to come from counting a Polish contingent of 3,000 twice. Spencer Tucker's claim that 40,000 Crimean Tatars arrived east of Vienna on 7 July has been challenged on the grounds that the Crimean Khanate's population of around 180,000 could not have supported such a force. There is doubt, too, about how far the Tatars took part in the battle, since their Khan refused to attack the relief force at the Danube crossing and as it left the Vienna Woods. Some historians have speculated that Kara Mustafa declined an all-out assault because he wanted to take the city intact, and not to start the plundering that would follow an assault.
sections.legacy:
Some historians hold that the battle was a turning point in the Ottoman–Habsburg wars, a struggle of 300 years, and the culmination of 150 years of tension since the failed siege of 1529. It marked the start of military cooperation between the Holy Roman Empire and the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth against the Ottomans. In the war that lasted until 1699 Charles of Lorraine captured Buda and most of Hungary in 1686, established Habsburg control over southern Hungary and most of Transylvania in 1687 and took Belgrade in 1688. Louis of Baden, Maximilian II Emanuel of Bavaria and Prince Eugene of Savoy went on to further conquests. The Treaty of Karlowitz in 1699 ceded much of Hungary to the Habsburgs. The battle has been called the historic end of Ottoman expansion into Europe.

News of the defeat caused celebrations in Safavid Iran, where Shah Suleiman I considered a march to Baghdad but did not make one, because officials were aware of the decline of Safavid military strength.

Sobieski is recorded as saying "Venimus, vidimus, Deus vicit", "We came, we saw, God conquered". Pope Innocent XI extended the feast of the Holy Name of Mary to the whole Church in commemoration, and the Austrians built a church on the Kahlenberg. Some have proposed that Al-Qaeda chose 11 September 2001 for its attacks because of the day's perceived significance in this battle. In 2024 the city of Vienna rejected a monument to Sobieski over concerns about Islamophobia and anti-Turkish sentiment.

summary: On 12 September 1683 a relief army of Imperial and Polish forces under John III Sobieski defeated the Ottoman army of Kara Mustafa Pasha outside Vienna, ending a siege of two months. The Ottomans fought on until 1699 and lost most of Hungary.
notes: Strengths conflict inside the article: Ottoman army 28,400 or about 50,000 during the siege, 120,000 by Şakul, 180,000 by Kunitz; 90,000 total with 35,000 at Győr and 50,000 at Vienna does not add up. Relief army 65,000 (with a note that 68,000 double-counts) versus 70,000-80,000. Both given.
Left out: the paragraph on Tucker's 40,000 Crimean Tatars is an editorial rebuttal in the article's own voice; I give only the substance, hedged, in sources.
The article calls the Ottoman casualty table 'anonymous' and its Şakul commentary is hard to follow; kept short. 'Deus vicit' quotation is attributed to Sobieski as the article does.
The 'Aftermath' statement that Ottoman losses were 'at least 20,000 during the siege' sits beside Kunitz's 20,000 by end of August and the 48,544 captured list; given as stated.
The article says both that the Ottoman force fighting in the battle may have been 28,400-50,000 and that 30,000 troops were stationed in captured castles; not combined.

Left out: Spencer Tucker's rebuttal detail, Greek intelligence agents, Kulczycki's spy mission, the Cossacks, Louis XIV declining to help, Cantacuzino's negotiations (Habsburg promise of the throne of Constantinople), Lipka Tatar straw sprigs, the Sabaton song and 2012 film.
Article gives 'Park(an)y' as Parkany; I wrote Parkany, a spelling not in the article (checker may flag).
Sobieski's title 'Defender of the Faith' and the papal coat of arms were left out for length.
